Figure 5: 3-D Rendition of the Maximum (3.9 MW) Add-On OTEC Design Coupled with a Generic Semi-Submersible Platform. 15 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 Figure 6: Elevation (Left) and Plan (Right) View of the Maximum (3.9 MW) Add-On OTEC Design. 16 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 The installation of the self-buoyant 3.9 MW Add on OTEC is similar to the smaller add-on facility in that it would be transported separately from the main platform, and added on after the main facility is moored in its permanent location. Due to the larger size, the expected added downward force on the larger connection brackets would need to be determined during the detailed design phase stability study. Since the major water handling equipment (pumps and heat exchangers) are located inside the large add-on hull column, there is an added risk of flooding the hull column (compared to that of the 1.0 MW concept). To limit the exposure, compartments should be built into the lower portions of the main hull column so that if a leak should flood a compartment, there would still be sufficient buoyancy to stabilize the add-on while the leak is addressed. The design includes double gate valves on all water inlets so that the leaking equipment can be isolated from the seawater, the compartment can be pumped out, and repairs can be completed. Similar to the 1.0 MW OTEC add-on arrangement previously described, there is a middle hull column that extends upward to the platform for personnel and small equipment access. It is envisaged that a freight elevator would be installed in the center hull column for personnel and small equipment to be transported to and from each of the levels in the OTEC add-on hull. Equipment selection to ensure maximum reliability for this case is more critical for this concept due to the difficulties of equipment removal. Although titanium heat exchangers will resist corrosion, fouling is also a consideration. Provisions for in place cleaning of the exchangers will add value over the life of the facility and are recommended. To remove the large CW and WW pumps and the condensers and evaporators, it will be necessary for the design to include provisions for lifting equipment inside the compartments of the add-on hull column and provide a passageway through the levels above to lift out the equipment using a crane. In addition, it may be necessary to remove adjacent equipment (such as a condenser to allow for the removal of an evaporator). The compartment walls would also need to have a removable water-tight passageway for equipment removal. The provisions for equipment removal are unavoidable as they will also need to be utilized for the initial construction of the OTEC plant.
